## **Background and Summary**

Psychological research depends fundamentally on the ability to measure the constructs it aims to study. While some constructs can be operationalised through observable indicators such as reaction times or physiological responses, the majority of psychological phenomena of interest, including self-esteem, anxiety, and cognitive ability, have no direct behavioural or biological analogue. Psychometric instruments therefore occupy a central role in psychological science, serving as the primary means through which internal, difficult-to-observe constructs are translated into quantifiable data. The quality of these instruments, and the transparency with which their development and validation are reported, is not merely a methodological concern but a prerequisite for the interpretability and accumulation of psychological knowledge.

Evidence that this prerequisite is routinely unmet has accumulated steadily across several decades. Early reviews identified widespread omissions in the reporting of validity and reliability evidence across counselling, educational, and applied psychology \[ @meier1990 ; @qualls1996 ; @slaney2009\] . @flake2017 examined a representative sample of articles published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that latent variable measurement was pervasive in social and personality research, yet construct validation evidence was almost universally absent. Cronbach's alpha was frequently the only psychometric property reported, and for a substantial minority of scales, no psychometric information was reported at all. @hussey2020 demonstrated that when 15 of the most widely used self-report measures in social and personality psychology were subjected to comprehensive validity assessment, including factor structure, test-retest reliability, and measurement invariance, only 4% demonstrated good validity, despite 88% appearing adequate based on internal consistency alone. The authors characterised this as a problem of hidden invalidity: a state of affairs in which the gap between what is reported and what is actually true of a measure is so large that the published literature cannot be trusted to reflect the psychometric quality of the tools it relies upon. Beyond self-report measures, @parsons2019 have argued that psychological science has not yet developed a tradition of routinely examining or reporting the reliability of cognitive-behavioural task measures, proposing that adopting such a practice as a field-wide standard is necessary to draw robust inferences from statistical analyses.

In response to these concerns, the field has developed a succession of formal standards and guidelines intended to anchor reporting practice. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, most recently revised in 2014 by the American Educational Research Association, the American Psychological Association, and the National Council on Measurement in Education, represent the most comprehensive framework for evaluating validity evidence, organised around five evidence categories: test content, response processes, internal structure, relations to other variables, and consequences of testing. The APA's updated Journal Article Reporting Standards, published in 2018, further codified expectations for the transparent reporting of measures used in quantitative research [@appelbaum2018]. @flake2020 subsequently consolidated growing concern about the gap between these standards and actual practice under the term questionable measurement practices (QMPs), arguing that insufficient transparency in measure development and validation undermines the evidentiary value of psychological findings in waysdefined that are structurally similar to, and in some respects more consequential than, the questionable research practices that have occupied the field's attention since the replication. One mechanism through which this occurs is the attenuation of replicability by measurement error. When psychometric instruments lack precision, the signal-to-noise ratio is reduced, diminishing statistical power and increasing the probability of Type II errors across independent studies [@loken2017]. @hedge2017 demonstrated formally that measures with poor reliability produce highly variable effect size estimates, making successful replication a statistical near-impossibility even when the underlying effect is genuine. Poor psychometric reporting thus does not merely obscure the quality of individual instruments; it structurally compounds the replication problem across the literature.

The replication crisis itself, catalysed most visibly by the [@estimati2015]'s finding that only 36% of 100 published psychological studies replicated successfully, prompted widespread methodological reform. Open science initiatives, including preregistration, registered reports, open data, and the Transparency and Openness Promotion guidelines [@nosek2015] , have been widely adopted across the field. @korbmacher2023 have argued that the period following the replication crisis is best understood not as a collapse of psychological science but as a credibility revolution, marked by structural, procedural, and community-driven improvements in research practice. Whether these developments have filtered through to the specific domain of psychometric reporting, however, is unknown. There has been no systematic empirical investigation of whether the quality of psychometric reporting for newly developed and modified measures has changed over time, and if so, whether any improvement has been genuine and broad-based or confined to particular validity evidence types, subfields, or journal strata.

This absence of evidence matters now more than ever. The proliferation of new measures, including ad hoc scales constructed for single studies, online survey adaptations of existing instruments, and cross-cultural modifications, has accelerated alongside the growth of online data collection platforms and increased research output. If poor reporting practices have persisted through the open science era despite the availability of explicit guidelines, this represents a fundamental and underappreciated threat to cumulative psychological science. If, on the other hand, reporting quality has genuinely improved, this constitutes important positive evidence that reform efforts have had downstream effects on measurement practice, and may help to identify which reform mechanisms have been most effective. The present study therefore aims to examine systematically whether the reporting quality of newly developed and modified psychometric measures has changed across the period 2002 to 2026, a window that spans both the pre-reform era and the substantive reform period that followed the replication crisis, using a large multi-subfield sample of published psychology articles.

**Primary Research Question**

The overarching aim of this review is to examine whether psychometric reporting practices have changed over time across psychology. Our primary and secondary research questions are as follows: 

1.  Has the overall quality of psychometric reporting for newly developed and modified measures improved over time (2002 to 2026)?

**Secondary research questions:**

2.  Has the type of validity evidence reported (e.g., dimensionality, internal consistency, convergent validity, discriminant validity, relations with other variables) changed over time?

<!-- -->

3.  Have specific development procedures (e.g., expert review, cognitive interviewing, piloting) of item generation changed overtime?

## Analysis Plan

Composite measures will be made by coding items and sub-items as 1 (yes/selected) or 0 (no/unselected). No distinction will be made as to whether information is in the main article or a supplement (both will be coded as yes). ‘Other’ responses will be coded as 1 (one or more responses) or 0 (left blank).

- **Descriptive information about scale construction:** Questions 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 relate to descriptions of how the scale develops. For Q9 where there are multiple items under 'yes' these will be scored as 1 (selected) and 0 (not selected). Q10.5 will be scored as (2) 'All items ..', (1) 'Example items ...' and (0) 'No items ...'. This will result in a total count from 0 (reported nothing) to 14 (reported everything that could feasibly be reported).

- **Participant descriptions:** Q12-Q14 relate to participant descriptions/missing data. Q12 has three sub-items scored in the normal way resulting (score range 0-3); Q13.2 scored treating location, administration and mode as sub-items so the range of scores will be 0-4. Q14 scored in the usual way. Potential range across these items is 0 (reported nothing) to 8 (reported everything).

- **Validity:** Q15.4 and Q15.5 each scored as 1 (they reported something) yielding a total ranging from 0 (not reported) to 2 (reported both convergent and discriminant).

- **Reliability:** Q15.3 scored as 1 for every item selected yielding a total ranging from 0 (nothing reported) to 4 (reported everything)

- **Dimensionality:** Different scores will be computed for EFA/PCA and CFA

  - ***FA/PC Dimensionality:*** If an EFA or PCA is reported then Q15.1 or Q15.3 items are summed (score 1 for everything selected) to yield a score from 0 to 10 (or more if multiple items are written in other)

  - ***CFA Dimensionality:*** For CFA Q15.2 items are summed (score 1 for everything selected) to yield a score from 0 to 6 (or more if multiple items are written in other)

- **Overall score (primary outcome):** to compute an overall score, we will sum the aforementioned scores and convert to a proportion of the potential total (which is 28 or 38 if FA/PC is selected, 34 if CFA has been selected and 44 if FA/PC and CFA are selected)

**For our first research question**, we are focused on gaining an understanding of how the overall quality of psychometric reporting has changed across the period 2002 to 2026. Our primary outcome is the proportion of selected items on the coding scheme within each article. Because this outcome is bounded between 0 and 1, the model fitted will be a Bayesian beta regression [@ferrari2004; @geller2026; @smithson2006] with piecewise linear trends, using 2014 as the breakpoint to reflect the increasing influence of open science reform movements:

$$\begin{aligned} g\left(\mu_i\right) &= \ln\left(\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}\right) =  \eta_i\\ \eta_i &= \beta_{0} + \beta_1\text{time}_{i} + \beta_2\left(\text{time}_{i}-12\right)\times \text{era}_{i}  \end{aligned}$$

where **time** is coded such that 2002 = 0 and subsequent years represent time elapsed since 2002, and **era** is a dummy variable coded 0 = pre-2014 and 1 = post-2014. When era = 0, the model reduces to ηi=β0+β1timei\eta\_i = \beta\_0 + \beta\_1\text{time}\_i ηi​=β0​+β1​timei​, so β1\beta\_1 β1​ captures the slope of reporting quality pre-2014. When era = 1, the slope becomes β1+β2\beta\_1 + \beta\_2 β1​+β2​; therefore β2\beta\_2 β2​ represents the *difference* in slope post-2014 relative to pre-2014.

Our hypotheses are directional. We expect reporting quality to be broadly flat in the pre-2014 era, so we predict β1≈0\beta\_1 \approx 0 β1​≈0. We expect a positive change in trajectory following the open science reforms of 2014, so we predict β2\>0\beta\_2 \> 0 β2​\>0, indicating that the slope post-2014 is steeper than the slope pre-2014.

**Priors.** The β\beta βs are expressed in log-odds units. Given the piecewise structure of the model and the 0–1 scale of the outcome, the prior should capture only values that are physically plausible as rates of change per unit time. A raw annual change of as much as δ=0.08\delta = 0.08 δ=0.08 (the maximum possible across a 12-year span from 0 to 1) translates to approximately β≤1.8\beta \leq 1.8 β≤1.8 in log-odds; considering also small decreases, the plausible range is approximately −0.6\<β\<1.8-0.6 \< \beta \< 1.8 −0.6\<β\<1.8. Because we do not expect proportions to decrease substantially, the prior should lean toward positive values. A distribution of N(0.5,0.25)N(0.5, 0.25) N(0.5,0.25) provides appropriate coverage of this range. For the intercept, we might reasonably expect articles to report 25–75% of items. The most extreme base rates of around 0.1 and 0.9 correspond to β0=ln⁡(0.1/0.9)=−2.2\beta\_0 = \ln(0.1/0.9) = -2.2 β0​=ln(0.1/0.9)=−2.2 and β0=ln⁡(0.9/0.1)=2.2\beta\_0 = \ln(0.9/0.1) = 2.2 β0​=ln(0.9/0.1)=2.2 respectively; a N(0,3)N(0, 3) N(0,3) distribution captures these extremes. Default flat priors will be used for the dispersion parameters, as these are peripheral to the research question.

This model cannot accommodate proportions of exactly 0 or 1. Although it is unlikely that any article would receive a proportion of 0 (no items reported) or 1 (all items reported), should such values be observed we will fit a zero-and-one-inflated beta (ZOIB) model, which estimates two additional parameters: the overall probability of an extreme score (α\alpha α) and the conditional probability that an extreme score is a 1 rather than a 0 (γ\gamma γ).

**For our second research question**, we are focused on whether the *type* of validity evidence reported has changed over time. Our analyses will consist of descriptive statistics for each validity category (dimensionality, internal consistency, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and relations with other variables), summarising the proportion of articles reporting each type of evidence per year or per era. Trends will be visualised using time series plots grouped by evidence type.

**For our third research question**, we are focused on whether specific item development procedures (e.g., expert review, cognitive interviewing, piloting) have changed over time. As with the second research question, our analyses will consist of descriptive statistics, summarising the frequency and proportion of articles reporting each procedure per year and per era (pre- vs. post-2014). Results will be presented visually and in tabular form to allow comparison across procedure types and across time.

## Data source(s) and data type(s)

Data will consist of peer-reviewed psychology papers which have been published between 2002-2026. These data will be coded using content analysis, and quantified.

There will be three levels of data: -

- Journal level data

  - (E.g, Publisher, JIF, cited half-life)

- Article level data o

  - (E.g., Year of publication, DOI, Open access status)

- Measure level data

  - (E.g., Single vs. Multi item, newly developed vs. Modification, type of validity and reliability evidence reported)

## Databases

All journal article data will be drawn randomly from the open source OpenAlex database. OpenAlex has good coverage of academic articles, with a database of records several magnitudes larger than that of Web of Science and Scopus (Culbert et al., 2025). OpenAlex also provides a free API with technical documentation for bulk data extraction from their database, allowing for detailed filtering and randomisation of papers extracted. Data regarding journal/publication metrics will be drawn from Clarivate’s Journal Citation Report (JCR) database, which at the time of writing was last updated October 15, 2025. To

avoid inadvertently filtering out interdisciplinary research papers published in non- psychology journals, we will draw from both the ‘Psychiatry/Psychology’ and ‘Social

Sciences, General’ JCR category groups. At the time of this pre-registrations publication, the JCR database has 5,969 academic journals across both the ‘Psychiatry/Psychology’ and ‘Social Sciences, General’ category groups.

## Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria

Data will be filtered against two sets of inclusion/exclusion criteria: one relating to paper level meta data and the other relating to journal level meta data. Paper level data will be retrieved and filtered first during the initial API call with the paper’s associated journal level data filtered following this.

1.  When article metadata is drawn from the OpenAlex database, the API call will contain the following inclusion/exclusions for retrieved journal articles:

- The journal article must have been published between 2002 and 2026

- The article must have a DOI and ISSN or eISSN

- The article must not have been retracted

- The article must have been indexed as being in a subfield of psychology

- The article must have been indexed as being of the type ‘article’

- The article must be written in English 2. Upon completion of the API call, duplicate articles will be removed. The journal ISSNs & eISSNs associated with the articles will be cross-referenced with the compiled list of academic journals and their associated journal metrics; any articles with ISSNs or eISSNs that fail to match with any journal will be excluded.

## Query strings

Below is an example API call that will be used to extract social psychology paper meta-data: [**https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=**](https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=)

**has_doi:true, is_retracted:false,**

**from_publication_date:2002-01-01, to_publication_date:2026-02-11,**

**concepts.wikidata:<https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q161272,>**

**primary_location.source.has_issn:true,**

**type:article,**

**language:en &sample=1000**0

## Screening

Most of the filtering process will be embedded within the API call; however, individual coders will further exclude articles that they code if the article: -

- Does not contain any newly generated/modified psychometric measures

- Explicitly states that all relevant psychometric measures are not intended for research use/purposes

Given that coders will have access to full text journal papers, it will not be possible to obscure any bibliographic fields (e.g., author names, title, abstract). To reduce bias in coding, coders who indicate that they were involved in the conception, design, analysis, or writing of an article or have any other potential conflicts of interest will be re-allocated to a different randomly selected article.

## Intercoder reliability

Prior to data collection, all coders will complete a pre-selected set of 10 calibration papers so that inter-coder reliability can be assessed. Intercoder reliability will also be assessed at the mid-point and end of data collection, this will consist of 3 pre-screened papers at both time points. We will calculate both Krippendorff’s alpha & percent agreement as metrics of inter-coder reliability, as Krippendorff’s alpha can produce lower reliability estimates when category usage is skewed. Our cut-off points for acceptable inter-coder reliability are ≥ 0.67 for Krippendorff’s alpha and ≥ 75% for percent agreement (Krippendorff, 2004). Coders who fall below both of these thresholds will be asked to pause coding and to attend a meeting to discuss their coding differences. They will then complete a new set of calibration papers and must meet the reliability criteria before resuming coding.

## Sampling & Sample Size

Because of the breadth of this study’s inclusion criteria, there are well over 1m papers which fall within our inclusion criteria at the time of this pre-registration. It would be impractical to filter all eligible papers manually. As such, a randomised subset of 10,000 papers will be drawn for each of 5 psychology subfields (clinical, applied, cognitive, developmental and social) using the OpenAlex API. This process will leave us with a starting sample of 50,000 journal articles before the removal of duplicate articles and articles without ISSNs/eISSNs that match any stored in the JCR database. We do not plan to filter and code all journals within our final dataset, as this will likely still number tens of thousands after filtering. The minimum sample size for fully coded articles will be \~1000, which conservatively mirrors the sample sizes utilised in previous studies with similar data collection methods @barry2013 . As we have no planned frequentist analyses, this is not a prescribed stopping point. Data collection will continue until the end of the data collection period. In the unlikely event that the \~1000 article minimum is not met within this timeframe; the data collection period may potentially be extended.
